explanations.explanation: Water it is, friend. The text says the water was plentiful at Aenon near Salim, and people kept coming to be baptized. Baptizing takes a lot of water, so John picked a spot that had it. I pick my bakery spot the same way, right next to the oven.

Shade sounds lovely, and anybody who has stood near a hot oven all day would vote for it. But the text never mentions shade. It says the water was plentiful there. Aenon was a water spot, not a nap spot.

Room is a fair guess when people keep coming, since crowds need space. But the text doesn't say a word about room. It gives the reason as plentiful water. I'd have guessed room too, honestly, because I always run out of counter.

Close, baker, but the text says the opposite. It says John had not yet been thrown into prison. So at this point John is still out baptizing, and that matters for everything he says next. Prison comes later.

That's right. The text says John had not yet been thrown into prison. So John is still free and still out baptizing while this scene plays out. It's a quick note, but it tells you where we are on the timeline.

That's the one. A dispute arose between John's disciples and a certain Jew over the issue of ceremonial washing. The text doesn't tell us who said what in the argument. It only names the topic, and that topic leads straight to the disciples going to John.

The Sabbath is a big topic in the Gospels, so I see why it came to mind. But it isn't what this argument is about. The text says the dispute was over ceremonial washing. Sometimes an argument just stays on one subject, which is more than I can say for my family group chat.

Taxes will start an argument anywhere, no doubt about it. But the text doesn't put the temple tax in this scene. The dispute was over ceremonial washing. Money talk will have to wait for another passage.

Right. They tell John, “…everyone is going to Him.” They're talking about the One John testified about, and they say it to John. I think those disciples sound a little rattled, but that's my guess, not the text. What matters is how John answers.

explanations.answer: Only a few are going to Him
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what they say, friend. The disciples tell John that everyone is going to Jesus. Nobody in that report is counting a few. It sounds like a crowd to me.

Ha, that would be a nicer report for John, wouldn't it? But the disciples say it the other way around. They say everyone is going to Jesus, not asking for John. John's next words are about where all of this comes from.

explanations.answer: A man can receive only what is given him from heaven
explanations.explanation: Yes. John replies, “A man can receive only what is given him from heaven.” He doesn't argue about the crowds or count heads. He starts with what is given from heaven. I could use that instinct the next time my batch doesn't rise.

explanations.answer: A man has to protect what he has built
explanations.explanation: That's what you'd expect a worried person to say, but John says nothing like it. He says, “A man can receive only what is given him from heaven.” Protecting what he has built isn't in his answer at all. He starts with what comes from heaven.

explanations.answer: A man should not baptize without a teacher
explanations.explanation: John doesn't go after how Jesus baptizes or who taught Him. His first words are “A man can receive only what is given him from heaven.” That line is about what is given from heaven. Teachers don't come up.

Not quite, baker. John reminds them that they can testify he said the opposite. He says, “I am not the Christ, but am sent ahead of Him.” So he says he's sent ahead, and he never claims to be the Christ.

That's right. John tells his disciples, “You yourselves can testify that I said, ‘I am not the Christ, but am sent ahead of Him.’” He's reminding them of something they already heard from him. He said he was sent ahead, not that he was the Christ.

Overjoyed, you got it. John says the friend of the bridegroom stands and listens for him, and is overjoyed to hear the bridegroom's voice. That's a happy kind of waiting, like hearing a loved one's key in the door. The friend is glad to hear that voice.

Afraid is a fair thing to guess when everybody's upset about the crowds. But John's wedding picture isn't scary at all. The friend of the bridegroom is overjoyed to hear his voice. It's a happy sound.

I get why sorry came to mind after that worried report. But John says the friend is overjoyed, not sorry. Hearing the bridegroom's voice makes the friend happy. It's a wedding, friend, and nobody there needs to apologize for being glad.

True, and that's John's own joy he's talking about. He says, “That joy is mine, and it is now complete.” He's the friend who stands and listens, and he takes the joy as his own. Nothing in what he says is missing.
Not this time, friend. John says it straight out: “That joy is mine, and it is now complete.” He calls the joy his own, and he calls it complete. Nothing in his words says it's partial.

explanations.answer: He must increase and I must decrease
explanations.explanation: Yes. John says, “He must increase; I must decrease.” That's his whole answer to the worried report, short and plain. He's the friend of the bridegroom, and he's glad to see the bridegroom take center stage.

explanations.answer: We must grow side by side
explanations.explanation: Side by side sounds friendly, but John doesn't say it. He says, “He must increase; I must decrease.” One goes up and the other goes down. It isn't a shared growth chart.

explanations.answer: I must lead and He must follow
explanations.explanation: That's backwards, baker. John says, “He must increase; I must decrease.” He doesn't ask to lead anyone, and he already told them he was sent ahead of Jesus. His words put Jesus first.
That's it. John says, “The One who comes from heaven is above all.” He sets that next to the one from the earth, who belongs to the earth. Two kinds of speakers, and only one is above all.

Close, but John gives that line to someone else. The one from the earth belongs to the earth and speaks as one from the earth. About the One from heaven, John says He is above all. Different speaker, different source.
That's a sensible guess, but John doesn't mention the prophets in these verses. He says the One who comes from heaven is above all. That's the whole comparison he's making. I'd keep it that simple.

Not what John says, baker. He says the One from heaven testifies to what He has seen and heard, “yet no one accepts His testimony.” So John says nobody accepts it, not everybody. It's a sad line, and it sets up the very next verse.
Right. John says the One from heaven testifies to what He has seen and heard, “yet no one accepts His testimony.” That's the opposite of everyone accepting it. It's a heavy line, so I'll let it sit.

That's the one. John says, “Whoever accepts His testimony has certified that God is truthful.” Certified means signed and sealed, like a stamp of approval. The person who accepts the testimony puts that stamp on it, and the stamp says God is truthful.

explanations.answer: That he has kept the law
explanations.explanation: That's a reasonable thing to guess, but John never says it here. He says, “Whoever accepts His testimony has certified that God is truthful.” The stamp is about God being truthful. Keeping the law doesn't come up.

explanations.answer: That he is ready to be baptized
explanations.explanation: Baptism is all over this passage, so I see why you'd pick it. But John's line is about something else. “Whoever accepts His testimony has certified that God is truthful.” That's what the person has certified.

explanations.answer: The One whom God has sent
explanations.explanation: Yes. John says, “For the One whom God has sent speaks the words of God…” The One God has sent speaks God's words. That's the same One from heaven he's been describing.

explanations.answer: The one who is from the earth
explanations.explanation: That's the other speaker, baker. John says the one from the earth belongs to the earth and speaks as one from the earth. The one who speaks the words of God is the One whom God has sent.

The friend of the bridegroom is John's own picture from earlier, the one who stands and listens. But in this verse, the one who speaks the words of God is the One whom God has sent. Same speech, different person. I'd mix those up too, since John's been talking nonstop.
Not this time, friend. John says, “The Father loves the Son and has placed all things in His hands.” That's all things, not just some. Nothing is left on the shelf.

Right. John says, “The Father loves the Son and has placed all things in His hands.” All things, with nothing held back. I once handed a neighbor a cookie box and kept half behind my back, and I felt terrible about it. This is nothing like that.
Yes. John says, “Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life.” Notice it's has, right now. It's a big promise in a short sentence.
A long life sounds good, and I'd take extra years in the bakery. But that isn't what John says. He says, “Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life.” Eternal is a whole different thing from long.
The temple comes up a lot in Scripture, so it's a natural guess. But John doesn't say it here. He says, “Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life.” That's what the believer has.

True. John says whoever rejects the Son will not see life, and “Instead, the wrath of God remains on him.” This is a heavy part, and I won't joke about it. John says it right after the promise of eternal life.

John does say it, friend. He says whoever rejects the Son will not see life, and “Instead, the wrath of God remains on him.” This is a heavy part, so I'll just say it plainly. It comes right after the promise for whoever believes.
